access_differences.http: All three use the same OData HTTP endpoint, 51 requests and 1074741 response body bytes; fresh HTTP client per scan.
access_differences.cds: ABAP uses internal Open SQL against CDS (50 nonempty packages); external clients use SAP ABAP ODBC over verified HTTPS (51 logical fetch attempts).
access_differences.native: ABAP uses its existing primary HANA ADBC connection; external clients use a separate read-only HANA principal. All use 51 logical fetch attempts.
access_differences.resource_limits: The 1 CPU/256 MiB limits apply to external clients. ABAP runs inside the shared SAP container and is not isolated to these limits.
access_differences.sql_connection_lifecycle: Persistent block connection, new cursor per scan. First connection is in warmup; final session teardown is outside the measured window.
access_differences.deadlines: External requests and ABAP HTTP use 10 seconds; every scan uses 120 seconds. ABAP CDS/ADBC cannot enforce the same per-call cancellation as external drivers.
access_differences.byte_metrics: SQL body_bytes=0 means no HTTP application response body metric, not zero network traffic.

methods.percentiles: Nearest rank within each measured block: sorted latency at one-based rank ceil(p*n).
methods.aggregation: Ordinary sample median and observed minimum–maximum of three main repetition statistics; scans are not treated as independent experimental repetitions.
methods.throughput: Successful complete scans × 5,000 / actual measured wall seconds; every slow scan remains in the denominator. Warmup failures remain separate availability observations; these capacity figures are conditional on completing warmup.
methods.confidence_intervals: Not estimated. Two or three repetitions provide observed ranges, not confidence intervals.
methods.temporal_axis: Within-block measured scan index preserves exact order. Summed scan times exclude loop overhead and are not timestamps.
methods.timer_resolution: ABAP emits integer milliseconds. Wall time minus summed scan timings includes bookkeeping and rounding; it is not an isolated loop-overhead measurement.

limitations: This compares complete local access paths. HTTP includes OData/SADL, authentication, sockets and JSON; CDS ODBC includes SQL-service and driver work; native HANA uses another database interface and restricted database identity.

HTTP constructs and closes a client per scan, reusing connections within that scan. SQL clients keep their connection across scans and open/close a query or cursor per scan. Warmup and final disconnect are outside measured SQL wall time.

ABAP CDS reads typed values internally and formats them in ABAP. The shared ODBC query projects exact decimal and ISO-date strings in SQL. Native HANA also returns a text projection. Common validation and hashing do not make those conversion costs equal.
Node.js and Rust have equal one-CPU/256-MiB container caps. ABAP runs inside the shared SAP system with service and database resources; its work process does not have a matching independent cap.

All applications share one host and SAP/database system, with one measured client active at a time. Balanced ordering reduces systematic drift; it does not remove thermal, caching, background-load or time effects.

Page/package counters describe application behavior: HTTP 51 responses, internal CDS 50 nonempty packages, SQL 51 fetch attempts including EOF. They are not a measured count of SQL statements or physical database round trips.
Only three repetitions per application were measured. No statistical winner, isolated language-speed ratio, production capacity or concurrent-write claim follows from this run.
This nine-path run and its raw evidence remain local; this run was not pushed to GitHub.
